lesson.title: Two goals at once
lesson.subtitle: Plans nobody beats, weights, and what a limit is worth

video.title: Two goals at once
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Farah Rahman — education lecturer (main character)
Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Dr Farah at a desk with two printed exam timetables side by side.
scenes.animation: The two plans slide in; the numbers highlight; a question mark appears.
scenes.narration: Two plans for exam week land on my desk. One finishes in four days, but nine pupils sit two exams on the same day. The other takes six days, and only one pupil does. Which plan is better?

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the Optimization track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: two goals at once, and how to choose between them in the open.

scenes.visual: A see-saw: ‘days’ on one end, ‘pupils with two exams’ on the other.
scenes.animation: The see-saw tips one way, then the other.
scenes.narration: When two goals pull apart, no plan wins on both. A shorter exam week means more pupils with two exams in a day. A gentler week takes longer. That’s a trade-off: to gain on one goal, you give up some of the other.

scenes.visual: A list of six plans; three get crossed out, three stay with ticks.
scenes.animation: Plans tick or cross as they are compared.
scenes.narration: Ms Salma lists six plans and drops any plan that another plan beats: no worse on either goal, and better on one. Plan C takes five days with six pupils clashing, but plan B also takes five days, with only four. So C goes. What’s left, plans A, B and D, is the Pareto front.

scenes.visual: Six dots on a chart of days against pupils; the three front dots join into a curve.
scenes.animation: Beaten dots fade; the front curve draws itself.
scenes.narration: A plan is on the Pareto front when no other plan is at least as good on every goal and better on one. Picking from the front isn’t maths any more. It’s a judgement about what matters more.

scenes.visual: Two balances: with the first weights D is lightest; with the second, B is.
scenes.animation: Scores count up under each plan; the winner glows.
scenes.narration: One way to choose is to give each goal a weight. Count one exam day as much as one clashing pupil, and plan D wins: six plus one is seven. Count a day as much as four clashing pupils, and plan B wins instead.

scenes.visual: A staff meeting: teachers, a pupil and a parent agree two weights on a flip chart.
scenes.animation: Weights are written; hands go up.
scenes.narration: So the weights decide, and weights are values, not facts. Agree them before you see the plans, with the people who carry the cost: teachers, pupils, parents. Then say them out loud.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma holds two cards, E and D. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Plan E takes seven days, with one pupil clashing. Plan D takes six days, also with one. Can E ever be the right choice?

scenes.visual: E is crossed out next to D. Then a padlock with a ‘+1’ tag appears.
scenes.animation: Cross badge pops; the padlock slides in.
scenes.narration: No: D is never worse and it’s shorter, so E is beaten, whatever the weights. Now a different trade-off. What is one more unit of a limit worth?

scenes.visual: The garden plan with three ‘+1’ buttons: hours, land, water; a bar chart of the gains.
scenes.animation: Bars grow one at a time; the water bar stays flat.
scenes.narration: In the school garden, the best plan earns two hundred and ninety. Give pupils one more hour a week, solve again, and it earns two hundred and ninety-five: an hour is worth five. One more bed of land is worth twenty-five. And more water is worth nothing, because three cans are already spare.

scenes.visual: A phone with the lab: the shaded garden plans, sliders for prices and hours, the best corner circled.
scenes.animation: A finger drags the tomato slider; the circled corner jumps.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: The best plan is at a corner
scenes.narration: In the app, open the garden plan. Raise the tomato price and watch the best corner jump. Then give pupils more hours, and see what the extra time buys.

scenes.visual: Dr Farah holds two price tags: a bed for 20, an hour for 10. Three answer cards appear.
scenes.narration: Your turn. The garden club can buy one more bed of land for twenty coins, or pay for one more hour of pupils’ time for ten. Which is worth buying?

scenes.visual: Four summary lines and a takeaway bar.
scenes.animation: Lines tick in; the takeaway slides up.
scenes.narration: The bed: it adds twenty-five for twenty coins, while an hour adds only five for ten. Remember: when goals pull apart, keep the plans nobody beats. Weights pick a plan, so agree them openly. And solve again to see what a limit is worth.

scenes.visual: Pupils in groups crossing out plan cards; one group presents its choice.
scenes.animation: Cards get crossed out; a hand goes up.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: give pupils four plans for sports day, each with two scores. Groups cross out every beaten plan. Then each group argues for one of the rest, and says which goal it weighted more.

checkpoints.prompt: Plan E: 7 days, 1 pupil clashing. Plan D: 6 days, 1 pupil. Can E be the right choice?

options.text: Yes, if days don’t matter much
Only if pupils vote for it
No: D is as good on one goal and better on the other

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — D ties on clashes and is a day shorter, so E is beaten whatever the weights.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — D is never worse than E and is one day shorter. A beaten plan can’t win with any weights.

checkpoints.prompt: One more bed for 20 coins, or one more hour for 10. Which is worth buying?

options.text: The bed: it adds 25 for 20 coins
Neither: the plan is already the best

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a bed adds 25 to the profit and costs 20, so it pays. An hour adds 5 and costs 10, so it doesn’t.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — compare what each adds with what it costs: a bed adds 25 for 20, an hour only 5 for 10.
